findings.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
findings.trigger: If an attacker provides a specially crafted input that includes shell metacharacters or control operators, it could potentially lead to OS command injection.
findings.assumptions: The program is intended to run in a context where it might be possible to inject shell commands, although it's not clear from the given code fragment.

findings.title: Integer Overflow or Wraparound
findings.trigger: If an attacker provides a very large value for N, it could cause an integer overflow when calculating the size for memory allocation (e.g., N * sizeof(int *), N * sizeof(int)).
findings.assumptions: The program does not check if the allocated memory size exceeds available system resources, which could lead to a crash or memory corruption.

findings.title: Use of Potentially Misleading Function
findings.trigger: The use of atoi() does not provide any error checking, so if the input is not a valid integer, it returns 0. This could lead to unexpected behavior or security issues.
findings.assumptions: The program assumes that the input will always be a valid integer, which may not be the case.

findings.title: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')
findings.trigger: If an attacker can control the values in matrices A and B, they might be able to inject malicious code or manipulate the program's behavior.
findings.assumptions: The program does not validate or sanitize the input matrices, which could lead to code injection vulnerabilities.
